passage: I'm Ankita, and last term my friend Keerthana changed so fast it scared me. She quit chess club, which she loved. She stopped sitting with us at lunch. In the April heat she wore a full-sleeved sweater every day. Then she handed me her whole set of sketch pens and said, "Keep them. I won't need them." Some people in our class group chat were joking that she was being dramatic. I didn't add anything. After school I walked home with her and said I'd noticed, and that I cared. She shrugged and said nothing was going to get better anyway. That scared me even more. I went straight back to school and found Ms Fernandes, our class teacher. She listened, thanked me, and phoned Keerthana's parents and the school counsellor before I'd even left the staffroom. Keerthana is getting help now. We're still friends.

qa.a: Her whole set of sketch pens.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's shrug and words scare Ankita even more?
qa.a: Saying nothing was going to get better sounded hopeless, so Ankita feared Keerthana might be in real danger.

qa.q: Which choice did Ankita make instead of joining the group-chat jokes?
qa.a: Ankita spoke to Keerthana privately with care, then went straight to the class teacher that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Ankita said it had been noticed and that someone cared?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt seen rather than mocked, even without being able to say much back.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing withdrawal, a sweater in the heat, giving things away and hopeless talk, and choosing caring attention and a teacher over gossip.

passage:
Coach's note, under-16 hockey squad, Tuesday. Coach Raghav.
For three weeks Jaya has skipped the warm-up jokes she usually leads and sat alone on the bench. Today she was suddenly bright and calm, and after practice she handed her new stick to a junior and said, "You'll use it more than me." She also had a bandaged wrist she wouldn't explain. Two players were whispering about it; I told them to stop, and to come to me whenever they're worried about a teammate.
What I did next: I asked Jaya to help me carry cones, and in the storeroom I told her what I'd noticed. I asked plainly whether she was thinking of hurting herself. She was quiet, then said, "Sometimes." I stayed with her, thanked her for telling me, and phoned the school counsellor, who came over within the hour. Her mother arrived soon after, and they went together to the counsellor's office.

qa.q: What did Jaya hand to a junior?
What worried Raghav about Jaya's sudden brightness?
qa.a: Raghav felt worried because, after three weeks of withdrawal, the sudden calm and giving away her new stick felt to Raghav like warning signs, not recovery.

qa.q: What was the key choice Raghav made in the storeroom?
qa.a: Raghav asked plainly whether Jaya was thinking of hurting herself, stayed with her and phoned the school counsellor at once.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jaya to be asked plainly in the storeroom?
qa.a: Jaya may have felt some relief at finally being seen; her quiet "Sometimes" suggests she had not been able to say it before.

grounding: It shows a coach noticing withdrawal, a sudden mood change, giving things away and an unexplained injury, and responding with care instead of letting gossip spread.
